(a contraction of Chenaniah), one of the Levites who assisted at the solemn purification of the people under Ezra. (<scripRef id="c-p98.1" passage="Nehemiah 9:4" parsed="|Neh|9|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.9.4">Nehemiah 9:4</scripRef>)

(length), a river in the “land of the Chaldeans.” (<scripRef id="c-p99.1" passage="Ezekiel 1:3" parsed="|Ezek|1|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.1.3">Ezekiel 1:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezekiel 3:15" id="c-p99.2" parsed="|Ezek|3|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.3.15">3:15</scripRef>,<scripRef passage="Ezekiel 3:23" id="c-p99.3" parsed="|Ezek|3|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.3.23">23</scripRef>) etc. It is commonly regarded as identical with the Habor, (<scripRef id="c-p99.4" passage="2 Kings 17:6" parsed="|2Kgs|17|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.17.6">2 Kings 17:6</scripRef>) and perhaps the Royal Canal of Nebuchadnezzar,—the greatest of all the cuttings in Mesopotamia.

(cord), one of the singular topographical terms in which the ancient Hebrew language abounded. We find it always attached to the region of Argob. (3:4,13,14; <scripRef id="c-p100.1" passage="1 Kings 4:13" parsed="|1Kgs|4|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.4.13">1 Kings 4:13</scripRef>)

(handful of sheaves), a king of Elam, in the time of Abraham, who with three other chiefs made war upon the kings of Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboim and Zoar, and reduced them to servitude. (<scripRef id="c-p101.1" passage="Genesis 14:17" parsed="|Gen|14|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.14.17">Genesis 14:17</scripRef>)

is mentioned only three times in the Bible, and on each occasion under a different name in the Hebrew. (<scripRef id="c-p102.1" passage="1 Samuel 17:18" parsed="|1Sam|17|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.17.18">1 Samuel 17:18</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p102.2" passage="2 Samuel 17:29" parsed="|2Sam|17|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.17.29">2 Samuel 17:29</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p102.3" passage="Job 10:10" parsed="|Job|10|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.10.10">Job 10:10</scripRef>) It is difficult to decide how far these terms correspond with our notion of cheese, for they simply express various degrees of coagulation. Cheese is not at the present day common among the Bedouin Arabs, butter being decidedly preferred; but there is a substance closely corresponding to those mentioned in <scripRef id="c-p102.4" passage="1Sam 17, 2" parsed="|1Sam|17|0|0|0;|1Sam|2|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.17 Bible:1Sam.2">1Sam 17, 2</scripRef>Sam 17, consisting of coagulated buttermilk, which is dried until it become quite hard, and is then ground; the Arabs eat it mixed with butter.
(perfection), (<scripRef id="c-p103.1" passage="Ezra 10:30" parsed="|Ezra|10|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.10.30">Ezra 10:30</scripRef>) one who had a strange wife.
(completed), (<scripRef id="c-p104.1" passage="Ezra 10:35" parsed="|Ezra|10|35|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.10.35">Ezra 10:35</scripRef>) another like the above.
• A man among the descendants of Judah.
• Ezri the son of Chelub, one of David’s officers. (1 Chronicles 27:26)

(capable), the son of Hezron. Same as Caleb. (<scripRef id="c-p106.1" passage="1 Chronicles 2:9" parsed="|1Chr|2|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.2.9">1 Chronicles 2:9</scripRef>,<scripRef passage="1 Chronicles 2:18" id="c-p106.2" parsed="|1Chr|2|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.2.18">18</scripRef>,<scripRef passage="1 Chronicles 2:42" id="c-p106.3" parsed="|1Chr|2|42|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.2.42">42</scripRef>)

(those who go about in black, i.e. ascetics). In the Hebrew applied to the priests of the worship of false gods. (<scripRef id="c-p107.1" passage="2 Kings 23:5" parsed="|2Kgs|23|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.23.5">2 Kings 23:5</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p107.2" passage="Hosea 10:5" parsed="|Hos|10|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.10.5">Hosea 10:5</scripRef>) in margin; (<scripRef id="c-p107.3" passage="Zephaniah 1:4" parsed="|Zeph|1|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zeph.1.4">Zephaniah 1:4</scripRef>)

(subduer), the national deity of the Moabites. (<scripRef id="c-p108.1" passage="Numbers 21:29" parsed="|Num|21|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.21.29">Numbers 21:29</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p108.2" passage="Jeremiah 48:7" parsed="|Jer|48|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.48.7">Jeremiah 48:7</scripRef>,<scripRef passage="Jeremiah 48:13" id="c-p108.3" parsed="|Jer|48|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.48.13">13</scripRef>,<scripRef passage="Jeremiah 48:46" id="c-p108.4" parsed="|Jer|48|46|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.48.46">46</scripRef>) In (<scripRef id="c-p108.5" passage="Judges 11:24" parsed="|Judg|11|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.11.24">Judges 11:24</scripRef>) he also appears as the god of the Ammonites. Solomon introduced, and Josiah abolished, the worship of Chemosh at Jerusalem. (<scripRef id="c-p108.6" passage="1 Kings 11:7" parsed="|1Kgs|11|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.11.7">1 Kings 11:7</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p108.7" passage="2 Kings 23:13" parsed="|2Kgs|23|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.23.13">2 Kings 23:13</scripRef>) Also identified with Baal-peor, Baalzebub, Mars and Saturn.
• Son of Bilhan, son of Jediael, son of Benjamin, head of a Benjamite house, (1 Chronicles 7:10) probably of the family of the Belaites. [Bela]
• Father or ancestor of Zedekiah the false prophet. (1 Kings 22:11,24; 2 Chronicles 18:10,23)

(established by the Lord), chief of the Levites when David carried the ark to Jerusalem. (<scripRef id="c-p110.1" passage="1 Chronicles 15:22" parsed="|1Chr|15|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.15.22">1 Chronicles 15:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chronicles 26:29" id="c-p110.2" parsed="|1Chr|26|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.26.29">26:29</scripRef>)
(hamlet of the Ammonites), a place mentioned among the town of Benjamin. (<scripRef id="c-p111.1" passage="Joshua 18:24" parsed="|Josh|18|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.18.24">Joshua 18:24</scripRef>)

(the hamlet), one of the four cities of the Gibeonites, (<scripRef id="c-p112.1" passage="Joshua 9:17" parsed="|Josh|9|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.9.17">Joshua 9:17</scripRef>) named afterwards among the towns of Benjamin. (<scripRef id="c-p112.2" passage="Ezra 2:25" parsed="|Ezra|2|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.2.25">Ezra 2:25</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p112.3" passage="Nehemiah 7:29" parsed="|Neh|7|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.7.29">Nehemiah 7:29</scripRef>)

(lyre), one of the sons of Dishon the Horite “duke.” (<scripRef id="c-p113.1" passage="Genesis 36:26" parsed="|Gen|36|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.36.26">Genesis 36:26</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p113.2" passage="1 Chronicles 1:41" parsed="|1Chr|1|41|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.1.41">1 Chronicles 1:41</scripRef>)
(axe-men), (Ezekiel 25:16) same as Cherethites.

(executioners) and of King David. (<scripRef id="c-p115.1" passage="2 Samuel 8:18" parsed="|2Sam|8|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.8.18">2 Samuel 8:18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Samuel 15:18" id="c-p115.2" parsed="|2Sam|15|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.15.18">15:18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Samuel 20:7" id="c-p115.3" parsed="|2Sam|20|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.20.7">20:7</scripRef>,<scripRef passage="2 Samuel 20:23" id="c-p115.4" parsed="|2Sam|20|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.20.23">23</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p115.5" passage="1 Kings 1:38" parsed="|1Kgs|1|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.1.38">1 Kings 1:38</scripRef>,<scripRef passage="1 Kings 1:44" id="c-p115.6" parsed="|1Kgs|1|44|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.1.44">44</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p115.7" passage="1 Chronicles 18:17" parsed="|1Chr|18|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.18.17">1 Chronicles 18:17</scripRef>) It is plain that these royal guards were employed as executioners., (<scripRef id="c-p115.8" passage="2 Kings 11:4" parsed="|2Kgs|11|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.11.4">2 Kings 11:4</scripRef>) and as couriers, (<scripRef id="c-p115.9" passage="1 Kings 14:27" parsed="|1Kgs|14|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.14.27">1 Kings 14:27</scripRef>) But it has been conjectured that they may have been foreign mercenaries, and therefore probably Philistines, of which name Pelethites may be only another form.

(cutting, ravine), the torrent-bed or wady in which Elijah hid himself during the early part of the three-years drought. (<scripRef id="c-p116.1" passage="1 Kings 17:3" parsed="|1Kgs|17|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.17.3">1 Kings 17:3</scripRef>,<scripRef passage="1 Kings 17:5" id="c-p116.2" parsed="|1Kgs|17|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.17.5">5</scripRef>) The position of the Cherith has been much disputed. The argument from probability is in favor of the Cherith being on the east of Jordan, and the name may possibly be discovered there.

apparently a place in Babylonia from which some persons of doubtful extraction returned to Judea with Zerubbabel. (<scripRef id="c-p117.1" passage="Ezra 2:59" parsed="|Ezra|2|59|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.2.59">Ezra 2:59</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p117.2" passage="Nehemiah 7:61" parsed="|Neh|7|61|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.7.61">Nehemiah 7:61</scripRef>)

The symbolical figure so called was a composite creature-form which finds a parallel in the religious insignia of Assyria, Egypt and Persia, e.g. the sphinx, the winged bulls and lions of Nineveh, etc. A cherub guarded paradise. (<scripRef id="c-p118.1" passage="Genesis 3:24" parsed="|Gen|3|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.3.24">Genesis 3:24</scripRef>) Figures of Cherubim were placed on the mercy-seat of the ark. (<scripRef id="c-p118.2" passage="Exodus 25:18" parsed="|Exod|25|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.25.18">Exodus 25:18</scripRef>) A pair of colossal size overshadowed it in Solomon’s temple with the canopy of their contiguously extended wings. (<scripRef id="c-p118.3" passage="1 Kings 6:27" parsed="|1Kgs|6|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.6.27">1 Kings 6:27</scripRef>) Those on the ark were to be placed with wings stretched forth, one at each end of the mercy-seat.” Their wings were to be stretched upwards, and their faces “towards each other and towards the mercy-seat.” It is remarkable that with such precise directions as to their position, attitude and material, nothing, save that they were winged, is said concerning their shape. On the whole it seems likely that the word “cherub” meant not only the composite creature-form, of which the man, lion, ox and eagle were the elements, but, further, some peculiar and mystical form. (Some suppose that the cherubim represented God’s providence among men, the four faces expressing the characters of that providence: its wisdom and intelligence (man), its strength (ox), its kingly authority (lion), its swiftness, far-sighted (eagle). Others, combining all the other references with the description of the living creatures in Revelation, make the cherubim to represent God’s redeemed people. The qualities of the four faces are those which belong to God’s people. Their facing four ways, towards all quarters of the globe, represents their duty of extending the truth. The wings show swiftness of obedience; and only the redeemed can sing the song put in their mouths in (<scripRef id="c-p118.4" passage="Revelation 5:8-14" parsed="|Rev|5|8|5|14" osisRef="Bible:Rev.5.8-Rev.5.14">Revelation 5:8-14</scripRef>)—ED).

(hopes), a place named as one of the landmarks on the west part of the north boundary of Judah, (<scripRef id="c-p119.1" passage="Joshua 15:10" parsed="|Josh|15|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.10">Joshua 15:10</scripRef>) probably Kesla, about six miles to the northeast of Ainshems, on the western mountains of Judah.
(increase), fourth son of Nahor. (<scripRef id="c-p120.1" passage="Genesis 22:22" parsed="|Gen|22|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.22.22">Genesis 22:22</scripRef>)
(idolatrous), a town in the extreme south of Palestine, (Joshua 15:30) 15 Miles southwest of Beersheba. In (Joshua 19:4) the name is Bethul.
By this word are translated in the Authorized Version two distinct Hebrew terms:

• Aron ; this is invariably used for the ark of the covenant, and, with two exceptions, for that only. The two exceptions alluded to are (a) the “coffin” in which the bones of Joseph were carried from Egypt, (Genesis 50:26) and (b) the “chest” in which Jehoiada the priest collected the alms for the repairs of the temple. (2 Kings 12:9,10; 2 Chronicles 24:8-11)
• Genazim, “chests.” (Ezekiel 27:24) only.

(Heb. ’armon .) (<scripRef id="c-p123.1" passage="Genesis 30:37" parsed="|Gen|30|37|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.30.37">Genesis 30:37</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p123.2" passage="Ezekiel 31:8" parsed="|Ezek|31|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.31.8">Ezekiel 31:8</scripRef>) Probably the “palm tree” (Platanus orientalis) is intended. This tree thrives best in low and rather moist situations in the north of Palestine, and resembles our sycamore or buttonwood (Platanus occidentalis).

(the loins), one of the towns of Issachar. (<scripRef id="c-p124.1" passage="Joshua 19:18" parsed="|Josh|19|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.19.18">Joshua 19:18</scripRef>) From its position int he lists it appears to be between Jezreel and Shunem (Salam).
(lying), a name which occurs but once, (Genesis 38:5) probably the same as Achzib.

(a javelin), the name which in (<scripRef id="c-p126.1" passage="1 Chronicles 13:9" parsed="|1Chr|13|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.13.9">1 Chronicles 13:9</scripRef>) is given to the threshing-floor at which the accident to the ark took place. In the parallel account in <scripRef id="c-p126.2" passage="2Sam 6" parsed="|2Sam|6|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.6">2Sam 6</scripRef> the name is given as NACHON.

The blessing of offspring, but especially of the male sex, is highly valued among all eastern nations, while a the absence is regarded as one of the severest punishments. (<scripRef id="c-p127.1" passage="Genesis 16:2" parsed="|Gen|16|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.16.2">Genesis 16:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Genesis 7:14" id="c-p127.2" parsed="|Gen|7|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.7.14">7:14</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p127.3" passage="1 Samuel 1:6" parsed="|1Sam|1|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.1.6">1 Samuel 1:6</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p127.4" passage="2 Samuel 6:23" parsed="|2Sam|6|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.6.23">2 Samuel 6:23</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p127.5" passage="2 Kings 4:14" parsed="|2Kgs|4|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.4.14">2 Kings 4:14</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p127.6" passage="Isaiah 47:9" parsed="|Isa|47|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.47.9">Isaiah 47:9</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p127.7" passage="Jeremiah 20:15" parsed="|Jer|20|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.20.15">Jeremiah 20:15</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p127.8" passage="Psalms 127:3" parsed="|Ps|127|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.127.3">Psalms 127:3</scripRef>,<scripRef passage="Psalms 127:5" id="c-p127.9" parsed="|Ps|127|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.127.5">5</scripRef>) As soon as the child was born it was washed in a bath, rubbed with salt and wrapped in swaddling clothes. (<scripRef id="c-p127.10" passage="Ezekiel 16:4" parsed="|Ezek|16|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.16.4">Ezekiel 16:4</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p127.11" passage="Job 38:9" parsed="|Job|38|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.38.9">Job 38:9</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p127.12" passage="Luke 2:7" parsed="|Luke|2|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.2.7">Luke 2:7</scripRef>) On the 8th day the rite of circumcision, in the case of a boy, was performed and a name given. At the end of a certain time (forty days if a son and twice as long if a daughter) the mother offered sacrifice for her cleansing. (<scripRef id="c-p127.13" passage="Leviticus 12:1-8" parsed="|Lev|12|1|12|8" osisRef="Bible:Lev.12.1-Lev.12.8">Leviticus 12:1-8</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p127.14" passage="Luke 2:22" parsed="|Luke|2|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.2.22">Luke 2:22</scripRef>) The period of nursing appears to have been sometimes prolonged to three years. (<scripRef id="c-p127.15" passage="Isaiah 49:15" parsed="|Isa|49|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.49.15">Isaiah 49:15</scripRef>) <scripRef id="c-p127.16" passage="2 Macc. 7:27" parsed="|2Macc|7|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Macc.7.27">2 Macc. 7:27</scripRef>. The time of weaning was an occasion of rejoicing. (<scripRef id="c-p127.17" passage="Genesis 21:8" parsed="|Gen|21|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.21.8">Genesis 21:8</scripRef>) Both boys and girls in their early years were under the care of the women. (<scripRef id="c-p127.18" passage="Proverbs 31:1" parsed="|Prov|31|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.31.1">Proverbs 31:1</scripRef>) Afterwards the boys were taken by the father under his charge. Daughters usually remained in the women’s apartments till marriage. (<scripRef id="c-p127.19" passage="Leviticus 21:9" parsed="|Lev|21|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.21.9">Leviticus 21:9</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p127.20" passage="Numbers 12:14" parsed="|Num|12|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.12.14">Numbers 12:14</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p127.21" passage="1 Samuel 9:11" parsed="|1Sam|9|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.9.11">1 Samuel 9:11</scripRef>) The authority of parents, especially of the father, over children was very great, as was also the reverence enjoined by the law to be paid to parents. The inheritance was divided equally between all the sons except the eldest, who received a double portion. (<scripRef id="c-p127.22" passage="Genesis 25:31" parsed="|Gen|25|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.25.31">Genesis 25:31</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Genesis 49:3" id="c-p127.23" parsed="|Gen|49|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.49.3">49:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Genesis 21:17" id="c-p127.24" parsed="|Gen|21|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.21.17">21:17</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p127.25" passage="Judges 11:2" parsed="|Judg|11|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.11.2">Judges 11:2</scripRef>,<scripRef passage="Judges 11:7" id="c-p127.26" parsed="|Judg|11|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.11.7">7</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p127.27" passage="1 Chronicles 5:1" parsed="|1Chr|5|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.5.1">1 Chronicles 5:1</scripRef>,<scripRef passage="1 Chronicles 5:2" id="c-p127.28" parsed="|1Chr|5|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.5.2">2</scripRef>) Daughters had by right no portion in the inheritance; but if a man had no son, his inheritance passed to his daughters, who were forbidden to marry out of the father’s tribe. (<scripRef id="c-p127.29" passage="Numbers 27:1" parsed="|Num|27|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.27.1">Numbers 27:1</scripRef>,<scripRef passage="Numbers 27:8" id="c-p127.30" parsed="|Num|27|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.27.8">8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Numbers 36:2" id="c-p127.31" parsed="|Num|36|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.36.2">36:2</scripRef>,<scripRef passage="Numbers 36:8" id="c-p127.32" parsed="|Num|36|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.36.8">8</scripRef>)
(like his father), a son of David by Abigail. [Abigail]

(pining, sickly), the son of Naomi and husband of Ruth. (<scripRef id="c-p129.1" passage="Ruth 1:2-5" parsed="|Ruth|1|2|1|5" osisRef="Bible:Ruth.1.2-Ruth.1.5">Ruth 1:2-5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ruth 4:9" id="c-p129.2" parsed="|Ruth|4|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ruth.4.9">4:9</scripRef>) (B.C. 1250.)

(enclosure), a place or country mentioned in conjunction with Sheba and Asshur. (<scripRef id="c-p130.1" passage="Ezekiel 27:23" parsed="|Ezek|27|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.27.23">Ezekiel 27:23</scripRef>)

(longing), a follower and probably a son, of Barzillai the Gileadite, who returned from beyond Jordan with David. (<scripRef id="c-p131.1" passage="2 Samuel 19:37" parsed="|2Sam|19|37|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.19.37">2 Samuel 19:37</scripRef>,<scripRef passage="2 Samuel 19:38" id="c-p131.2" parsed="|2Sam|19|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.19.38">38</scripRef>,<scripRef passage="2 Samuel 19:40" id="c-p131.3" parsed="|2Sam|19|40|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.19.40">40</scripRef>) (B C 1023.) David appears to have bestowed on him a possession at Bethlehem, on which, in later times, an inn or khan was standing. (<scripRef id="c-p131.4" passage="Jeremiah 41:17" parsed="|Jer|41|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.41.17">Jeremiah 41:17</scripRef>)

(circuit), accurately Cinnareth, a fortified city in the tribe of Naphtali, (<scripRef id="c-p133.1" passage="Joshua 19:35" parsed="|Josh|19|35|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.19.35">Joshua 19:35</scripRef>) only, of which no trace is found in later writers, and no remains by travellers.

(<scripRef id="c-p134.1" passage="Numbers 34:11" parsed="|Num|34|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.34.11">Numbers 34:11</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p134.2" passage="Joshua 13:27" parsed="|Josh|13|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.13.27">Joshua 13:27</scripRef>) the inland sea, which is most similarly known to us as the “Lake of Gennesareth” or “Sea of Galilee.”

<term id="c-p147.12">Chronicles, First And Second Books Of</term>

the name originally given to the record made by the appointed historiographers in the kingdoms of Israel and Judah. In the LXX. these books are called Paralipomena (i.e. things omitted), which is understood as meaning that they are supplementary to the books of Kings. The constant tradition of the Jews is that these books were for the most part compiled by Ezra. One of the greatest difficulties connected with the captivity and return must have been the maintenance of that genealogical distribution of the land which yet was a vital point of the Jewish economy. To supply this want and that each tribe might secure the inheritance of its fathers on its return was one object of the author of these books. Another difficulty intimately connected with the former was the maintenance of the temple services at Jerusalem. Zerubbabel, and after him Ezra and Nehemiah, labored most earnestly to restore the worship of God among the people, and to reinfuse something of national life and spirit into their hearts. Nothing could more effectually aid these designs than setting before the people a compendious history of the kingdom of David, its prosperity under God; the sins that led to its overthrow; the captivity and return. These considerations explain the plan and scope of that historical work which consists of the two books of Chronicles. The first book contains the sacred history by genealogies from the Creation to David, including an account of David’s reign. In the second book he continues the story, giving the history of the kings of Judah, without those of Israel, down to the return from the captivity. As regards the materials used by Ezra, they are not difficult to discover. The genealogies are obviously transcribed from some register in which were preserved the genealogies of the tribes and families drawn up at different times; while the history is mainly drawn from the same document as those used in the books of King. [Kings, First And Second Books Of, BOOKS OF]
By this term we understand the technical and historical chronology of the Jews and their ancestors from the earliest time to the close of the New Testament Canon.
• TECHNICAL CHRONOLOGY.—The technical part of Hebrew chronology presents great difficulties.

• HISTORICAL CHRONOLOGY.—The historical part of Hebrew chronology is not less difficult than the technical. The information in the Bible is indeed direct rather than inferential although there is very important evidence of the latter kind, but the present state of the numbers make absolute certainty in many cases impossible. Three principal systems of biblical chronology have been founded, which may be termed (the Long System, the short, and the Rabbinical. There is a fourth, which although an off shoot in part of the last, can scarcely be termed biblical, in as much as it depends for the most part upon theories, not only independent of but repugnant to the Bible: this last is at present peculiar to Baron Bunsen. The principal advocates of the Long chronology are Jackson. Hales and Des-Vignoles. Of the Short chronology Ussher may be considered as the most able advocate The Rabbinical chronology accept the biblical numbers, but makes the most arbitrary corrections. For the date of the Exodus it has been virtually accepted by Bunsen, Lepsius and Lord A. Hervey. The numbers given by the LXX. for the antediluvian patriarchs would place the creation of Adam 2262 years before the end of the flood or B.C. cir. 5361 or 5421.

• Ecclesia (ekklesia) the Greek word for church, originally meant an assembly called out by the magistrate, or by legitimate authority. It was in this last sense that the word was adapted and applied by the writers of the New Testament to the Christian congregation. In the one Gospel of St. Matthew the church is spoken of no less than thirty-six times as “the kingdom.” Other descriptions or titles are hardly found in the evangelists. It is Christ’s household, (Matthew 10:25) the salt and light of the world, (Matthew 5:13,15) Christ’s flock, (Matthew 26:31; John 10:15) its members are the branches growing on Christ the Vine, John 15; but the general description of it, not metaphorical but direct, is that it is a kingdom, (Matthew 16:19) From the Gospel then we learn that Christ was about to establish his heavenly kingdom on earth, which was to be the substitute for the Jewish Church and kingdom, now doomed to destruction (Matthew 21:43) The day of Pentecost is the birthday of the Christian church. Before they had been individual followers Jesus; now they became his mystical body, animated by his spirit. On the evening of the day of Pentecost, the 3140 members of which the Church consisted were— (1) Apostles; (2) previous Disciples; (3) Converts. In (Acts 2:41) we have indirectly exhibited the essential conditions of church communion. They are (1) Baptism, baptism implying on the part of the recipient repentance and faith; (2) Apostolic Doctrine; (3) Fellowship with the Apostles; (4) The Lord’s Supper; (5) Public Worship. The real Church consists of all who belong to the Lord Jesus Christ as his disciples, and are one in love, in character, in hope, in Christ as the head of all, though as the body of Christ it consists of many parts.

was peculiarly, though not exclusively, a Jewish rite. It was enjoined upon Abraham, the father of the nation, by God, at the institution and as the token of the covenant, which assured to him and his descendants the promise of the Messiah. <scripRef id="c-p162.1" passage="Gen. 17" parsed="|Gen|17|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.17">Gen. 17</scripRef>. It was thus made a necessary condition of Jewish nationality. Every male child was to be circumcised when eight days old, (<scripRef id="c-p162.2" passage="Leviticus 12:3" parsed="|Lev|12|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.12.3">Leviticus 12:3</scripRef>) on pain of death. The biblical notice of the rite describes it as distinctively Jewish; so that in the New Testament “the circumcision” and “the uncircumcision” are frequently used as synonyms for the Jews and the Gentiles. The rite has been found to prevail extensively in both ancient and modern times. Though Mohammed did not enjoin circumcision in the Koran, he was circumcised himself, according to the custom of his country; and circumcision is now as common among the Mohammedans as among the Jews. The process of restoring a circumcised person to his natural condition by a surgical operation was sometimes undergone. Some of the Jews in the time of Antiochus Epiphanes, wishing to assimilate themselves to the heathen around them, “made themselves uncircumcised.” Against having recourse to this practice, from an excessive anti-Judaistic tendency, St. Paul cautions the Corinthians. a receptacle for water, either conducted from an external spring or proceeding from rain-fall. The dryness of the summer months and the scarcity of springs in Judea made cisterns a necessity, and they are frequent throughout the whole of Syria and Palestine. On the long-forgotten way from Jericho to Bethel, “broken cisterns” of high antiquity are found at regular intervals. Jerusalem depends mainly for water upon its cisterns, of which almost every private house possesses one or more, excavated in the rock on which the city is built. The cisterns have usually a round opening at the top, sometimes built up with stonework above and furnished with a curb and a wheel for a bucket. (<scripRef id="c-p164.1" passage="Ecclesiastes 12:6" parsed="|Eccl|12|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eccl.12.6">Ecclesiastes 12:6</scripRef>) Empty cisterns were sometimes used as prisons and places of confinement. The shelter given, and refreshment of rain promised, by clouds give them their peculiar prominence in Oriental imagery. When a cloud appears rain is ordinarily apprehended, and thus the “cloud without rain” becomes a proverb for the man of promise without performance. (<scripRef id="c-p179.1" passage="Proverbs 16:15" parsed="|Prov|16|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.16.15">Proverbs 16:15</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p179.2" passage="Isaiah 18:4" parsed="|Isa|18|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.18.4">Isaiah 18:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isaiah 25:5" id="c-p179.3" parsed="|Isa|25|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.25.5">25:5</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p179.4" passage="Jude 1" parsed="|Jude|1|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jude.1.1">Jude 1</scripRef>:12) comp. <scripRef id="c-p179.5" passage="Prov 25:14" parsed="|Prov|25|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.25.14">Prov 25:14</scripRef> The cloud is a figure of transitoriness, (<scripRef id="c-p179.6" passage="Job 30:15" parsed="|Job|30|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.30.15">Job 30:15</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p179.7" passage="Hosea 6:4" parsed="|Hos|6|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.6.4">Hosea 6:4</scripRef>) and of whatever intercepts divine favor or human supplication. (<scripRef id="c-p179.8" passage="Lamentations 2:1" parsed="|Lam|2|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lam.2.1">Lamentations 2:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lamentations 3:44" id="c-p179.9" parsed="|Lam|3|44|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lam.3.44">3:44</scripRef>) A bright cloud at times visited and rested on the mercy-seat. (<scripRef id="c-p179.10" passage="Exodus 29:42" parsed="|Exod|29|42|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.29.42">Exodus 29:42</scripRef>,<scripRef passage="Exodus 29:43" id="c-p179.11" parsed="|Exod|29|43|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.29.43">43</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p179.12" passage="1 Kings 8:10" parsed="|1Kgs|8|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.8.10">1 Kings 8:10</scripRef>,<scripRef passage="1 Kings 8:11" id="c-p179.13" parsed="|1Kgs|8|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.8.11">11</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p179.14" passage="2 Chronicles 5:14" parsed="|2Chr|5|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.5.14">2 Chronicles 5:14</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p179.15" passage="Ezekiel 43:4" parsed="|Ezek|43|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.43.4">Ezekiel 43:4</scripRef>) and was by later writers named Shechinah.

The pillar of cloud by day and of fire by night that God caused to pass before the camp of the children of Israel when in the wilderness. The cloud, which became a pillar when the host moved, seems to have rested at other times on the tabernacle, whence god is said to have “come down in the pillar.” (<scripRef id="c-p180.1" passage="Numbers 12:5" parsed="|Num|12|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.12.5">Numbers 12:5</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p180.2" passage="Exodus 33:9" parsed="|Exod|33|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.33.9">Exodus 33:9</scripRef>,<scripRef passage="Exodus 33:10" id="c-p180.3" parsed="|Exod|33|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.33.10">10</scripRef>) It preceded the host, apparently resting on the ark which led the way. (<scripRef id="c-p180.4" passage="Exodus 13:21" parsed="|Exod|13|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.13.21">Exodus 13:21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Exodus 40:36" id="c-p180.5" parsed="|Exod|40|36|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.40.36">40:36</scripRef>) etc.; <scripRef id="c-p180.6" passage="Numb 9:15-23" parsed="|Num|9|15|9|23" osisRef="Bible:Num.9.15-Num.9.23">Numb 9:15-23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Numb 10:34" id="c-p180.7" parsed="|Num|10|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.10.34">10:34</scripRef>

(nidus), a city of great consequence, situated at the extreme south west of the peninsula of Asia Minor, on a promontory now called Cape Crio, which projects between the islands of Cos and Rhodes. See (<scripRef id="c-p182.1" passage="Acts 21:1" parsed="|Acts|21|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.21.1">Acts 21:1</scripRef>) It is now in ruins.

The first and most frequent use of the word rendered coal is a live ember, burning fuel. (<scripRef id="c-p183.1" passage="Proverbs 26:21" parsed="|Prov|26|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.26.21">Proverbs 26:21</scripRef>) In (<scripRef id="c-p183.2" passage="2 Samuel 22:9" parsed="|2Sam|22|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.22.9">2 Samuel 22:9</scripRef>,<scripRef passage="2 Samuel 22:13" id="c-p183.3" parsed="|2Sam|22|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.22.13">13</scripRef>) “coals of fire” are put metaphorically for the lightnings proceeding from God. (<scripRef id="c-p183.4" passage="Psalms 18:8" parsed="|Ps|18|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.18.8">Psalms 18:8</scripRef>,<scripRef passage="Psalms 18:12" id="c-p183.5" parsed="|Ps|18|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.18.12">12</scripRef>,<scripRef passage="Psalms 18:13" id="c-p183.6" parsed="|Ps|18|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.18.13">13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Psalms 140:10" id="c-p183.7" parsed="|Ps|140|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.140.10">140:10</scripRef>) In (<scripRef id="c-p183.8" passage="Proverbs 26:21" parsed="|Prov|26|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.26.21">Proverbs 26:21</scripRef>) fuel not yet lighted is clearly signified. The fuel meant in the above passage is probably charcoal, and not coal in our sense of the word.
border, with no more reference to lands bordering on the sea than to any other bordering lands.

(<scripRef id="c-p186.1" passage="Matthew 26:34" parsed="|Matt|26|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.26.34">Matthew 26:34</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p186.2" passage="Mark 13:35" parsed="|Mark|13|35|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.13.35">Mark 13:35</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 14:30" id="c-p186.3" parsed="|Mark|14|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.14.30">14:30</scripRef>) etc. The domestic cock and hen were early known to the ancient Greeks and Romans, and as no mention is made in the Old Testament of these birds, and no figures of them occur on the Egyptian monuments, they probably came into Judea with the Romans, who, as is well known, prized these birds both as articles of food and for cock-fighting.
probably signifies bad weeds or fruit. (<scripRef id="c-p188.1" passage="Job 31:40" parsed="|Job|31|40|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.31.40">Job 31:40</scripRef>)

(hollow Syria), the remarkable valley or hollow which intervenes between Libanus and Anti-Libanus, stretching a distance of nearly a hundred miles. The only mention of the region as a separate tract of country which the Jewish Scriptures contain is probably that in (<scripRef id="c-p189.1" passage="Amos 1:5" parsed="|Amos|1|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Amos.1.5">Amos 1:5</scripRef>) where “the inhabitants of the plain of Aven” are threatened in conjunction with those of Damascus. The word is given in the Authorized Version as CELO-SYRIA.

(argaz), a movable box hanging from the side of a cart. (<scripRef id="c-p190.1" passage="1 Samuel 6:8" parsed="|1Sam|6|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.6.8">1 Samuel 6:8</scripRef>,<scripRef passage="1 Samuel 6:11" id="c-p190.2" parsed="|1Sam|6|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.6.11">11</scripRef>,<scripRef passage="1 Samuel 6:15" id="c-p190.3" parsed="|1Sam|6|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.6.15">15</scripRef>) The word is found nowhere else.

(all-seeing), a man of the tribe of Judah in the time of Nehemiah. (<scripRef id="c-p192.1" passage="Nehemiah 3:15" parsed="|Neh|3|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.3.15">Nehemiah 3:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Nehemiah 11:5" id="c-p192.2" parsed="|Neh|11|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.11.5">11:5</scripRef>) (B.C. 536.)
For the proper sense of this term, as it occurs in (Judges 8:26) see Earrings.

In (<scripRef id="c-p194.1" passage="2 Kings 22:14" parsed="|2Kgs|22|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.22.14">2 Kings 22:14</scripRef>) it is probable that the word translated “college” represents here not an institution of learning, but that part of Jerusalem known as the “lower city” or suburb, built on the hill Akra, including the Bezetha or new city.

a designation of Philippi, in (<scripRef id="c-p195.1" passage="Acts 16:12" parsed="|Acts|16|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.16.12">Acts 16:12</scripRef>) After the battle of Actium, Augustus assigned to his veterans those parts of Italy which had espoused the cause of Antony, and transported many of the expelled inhabitants to Philippi, Dyrrhachium and other cities. In this way Philippi was made a Roman colony with the “Jus Italicum.” At first the colonists were all Roman citizens, and entitled to vote at Rome.

The terms relative to color, occurring in the Bible, may be arranged in two classes, the first including those applied to the description of natural objects, the second those artificial mixtures which were employed in dyeing or painting. The purple and the blue were derived from a small shellfish found in the Mediterranean, and were very costly, and hence they were the royal colors. Red, both scarlet and crimson, was derived from an insect resembling the cochineal. The natural colors noticed in the Bible are white, black, red, yellow and green. The only fundamental color of which the Hebrews appear to have had a clear conception was red ; and even this is not very often noticed.

more properly Colos’sae, was a city of Phrygia in Asia Minor, in the upper part of the basin of the Maeander, on the Lycus. Hierapolis and Laodicea were in its immediate neighborhood. (<scripRef id="c-p197.1" passage="Colossians 1:2" parsed="|Col|1|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Col.1.2">Colossians 1:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Colossians 4:13" id="c-p197.2" parsed="|Col|4|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Col.4.13">4:13</scripRef>,<scripRef passage="Colossians 4:15" id="c-p197.3" parsed="|Col|4|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Col.4.15">15</scripRef>,<scripRef passage="Colossians 4:16" id="c-p197.4" parsed="|Col|4|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Col.4.16">16</scripRef>) see Reve 1:11; 3:14 St. Paul is supposed by some to have visited Colosse and founded or confirmed the Colossian church on his third missionary journey. (<scripRef id="c-p197.5" passage="Acts 18:23" parsed="|Acts|18|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.18.23">Acts 18:23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 19:1" id="c-p197.6" parsed="|Acts|19|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.19.1">19:1</scripRef>)

was written by the apostle St. Paul during his first captivity at Rome. (<scripRef id="c-p198.1" passage="Acts 28:16" parsed="|Acts|28|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.28.16">Acts 28:16</scripRef>) (A.D. 62.) The epistle was addressed to Christians of the city of Colosse, and was delivered to them by Tychicus, whom the apostle had sent both to them, (<scripRef id="c-p198.2" passage="Colossians 4:7" parsed="|Col|4|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Col.4.7">Colossians 4:7</scripRef>,<scripRef passage="Colossians 4:8" id="c-p198.3" parsed="|Col|4|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Col.4.8">8</scripRef>) and to the church of Ephesus, (<scripRef id="c-p198.4" passage="Ephesians 6:21" parsed="|Eph|6|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.6.21">Ephesians 6:21</scripRef>) to inquire into their state and to administer exhortation and comfort. The main object of the epistle is to warn the Colossians against the spirit of semi-Judaistic and semi-Oriental philosophy which was corrupting the simplicity of their belief, and was noticeably tending to obscure the eternal glory and dignity of Christ. The similarity between this epistle and that to the Ephesians is striking. The latter was probably written at a later date.

(<scripRef id="c-p199.1" passage="John 14:16" parsed="|John|14|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.14.16">John 14:16</scripRef>) The name given by Christ to the Holy Spirit. The original word is Paraclete, and means first Advocate, a defender, helper, strengthener, as well as comforter.

From the time that men began to live in cities, trade, in some shape, must have been carried on to supply the town-dwellers with necessaries from foreign as well as native sources, for we find that Abraham was rich, not only in cattle, but in silver, gold and gold and silver plate and ornaments. (<scripRef id="c-p200.1" passage="Genesis 13:2" parsed="|Gen|13|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.13.2">Genesis 13:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Genesis 24:22" id="c-p200.2" parsed="|Gen|24|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.24.22">24:22</scripRef>,<scripRef passage="Genesis 24:53" id="c-p200.3" parsed="|Gen|24|53|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.24.53">53</scripRef>) Among trading nations mentioned in Scripture, Egypt holds in very early times a prominent position. The internal trade of the Jews, as well as the external, was much promoted by the festivals, which brought large numbers of persons to Jerusalem. (<scripRef id="c-p200.4" passage="1 Kings 8:63" parsed="|1Kgs|8|63|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.8.63">1 Kings 8:63</scripRef>) The places of public market were chiefly the open spaces near the gates, to which goods were brought for sale by those who came from the outside. (<scripRef id="c-p200.5" passage="Nehemiah 13:15" parsed="|Neh|13|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.13.15">Nehemiah 13:15</scripRef>,<scripRef passage="Nehemiah 13:16" id="c-p200.6" parsed="|Neh|13|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.13.16">16</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p200.7" passage="Zephaniah 1:10" parsed="|Zeph|1|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zeph.1.10">Zephaniah 1:10</scripRef>) The traders in later times were allowed to intrude into the temple, in the outer courts of which victims were publicly sold for the sacrifice. (<scripRef id="c-p200.8" passage="Zechariah 14:21" parsed="|Zech|14|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zech.14.21">Zechariah 14:21</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p200.9" passage="Matthew 21:12" parsed="|Matt|21|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.21.12">Matthew 21:12</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p200.10" passage="John 2:14" parsed="|John|2|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.2.14">John 2:14</scripRef>)

(made by Jehovah), one of the chiefs of the Levites in the time of Josiah. (<scripRef id="c-p201.1" passage="2 Chronicles 35:9" parsed="|2Chr|35|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.35.9">2 Chronicles 35:9</scripRef>) (B.C. 628).

The difference between wife and concubine was less marked among the Hebrews than among us, owing to the absence of moral stigma. The difference probably lay in the absence of the right of the bill of divorce, without which the wife could not be repudiated. With regard to the children of wife and of concubine, there was no such difference as our illegitimacy implies. The latter were a supplementary family to the former; their names occur in the patriarchal genealogies, (<scripRef id="c-p202.1" passage="Genesis 22:24" parsed="|Gen|22|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.22.24">Genesis 22:24</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p202.2" passage="1 Chronicles 1:22" parsed="|1Chr|1|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.1.22">1 Chronicles 1:22</scripRef>) and their position and provision would depend on the father’s will. (<scripRef id="c-p202.3" passage="Genesis 25:6" parsed="|Gen|25|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.25.6">Genesis 25:6</scripRef>) The state of concubinage is assumed and provided for by the law of Moses. A concubine would generally be either (1) a Hebrew girl bought of her father; (2) a Gentile captive taken in war; (3) a foreign slave bought; or (4) a Canaanitish woman, bond or free. The rights of the first two were protected by the law, (<scripRef id="c-p202.4" passage="Exodus 21:7" parsed="|Exod|21|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.21.7">Exodus 21:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Exodus 21:10-14" id="c-p202.5" parsed="|Exod|21|10|21|14" osisRef="Bible:Exod.21.10-Exod.21.14">21:10-14</scripRef>) but the third was unrecognized and the fourth prohibited. Free Hebrew women also might become concubines. To seize on royal concubines for his use was probably the intent of Abner’s act, (<scripRef id="c-p202.6" passage="2 Samuel 3:7" parsed="|2Sam|3|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.3.7">2 Samuel 3:7</scripRef>) and similarly the request on behalf of Adonijah was construed. (<scripRef id="c-p202.7" passage="1 Kings 2:21-24" parsed="|1Kgs|2|21|2|24" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.2.21-1Kgs.2.24">1 Kings 2:21-24</scripRef>)

meaning an aqueduct or trench through which water was carried. Tradition, both oral and as represented by Talmudical writers, ascribes to Solomon the formation of the original aqueduct by which water was brought to Jerusalem.

(shaphan), a gregarious animal of the class Pachydermata, which is found in Palestine, living in the caves and clefts of the rocks, and has been erroneously identified with the rabbit or coney. Its scientific name as Hyrax syriacus . The hyrax satisfies exactly the expressions in (<scripRef id="c-p204.1" passage="Psalms 104:18" parsed="|Ps|104|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.104.18">Psalms 104:18</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p204.2" passage="Proverbs 30:26" parsed="|Prov|30|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.30.26">Proverbs 30:26</scripRef>) Its color is gray or brown on the back, white on the belly; it is like the alpine marmot, scarcely of the size of the domestic cat, having long hair, a very short tail and round ears. It is found on Lebanon and in the Jordan and Dead Sea valleys.

This describes the Hebrew people in its collective capacity under its peculiar aspect as a holy community, held together by religious rather than political bonds. Sometimes it is used in a broad sense as inclusive of foreign settlers, (<scripRef id="c-p205.1" passage="Exodus 12:19" parsed="|Exod|12|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.12.19">Exodus 12:19</scripRef>) but more properly as exclusively appropriate to the Hebrew element of the population. (<scripRef id="c-p205.2" passage="Numbers 15:15" parsed="|Num|15|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.15.15">Numbers 15:15</scripRef>) The congregation was governed by the father or head of each family and tribe. The number of these representatives being inconveniently large for ordinary business, a further selection was made by Moses of 70, who formed a species of standing committee. (<scripRef id="c-p205.3" passage="Numbers 11:16" parsed="|Num|11|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.11.16">Numbers 11:16</scripRef>) Occasionally indeed the whole body of people was assembled at the door of the tabernacle, hence usually called the tabernacle of the congregation. (<scripRef id="c-p205.4" passage="Numbers 10:3" parsed="|Num|10|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.10.3">Numbers 10:3</scripRef>) The people were strictly bound by the acts of their representatives, even in cases where they disapproved of them. (<scripRef id="c-p205.5" passage="Joshua 9:18" parsed="|Josh|9|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.9.18">Joshua 9:18</scripRef>)

(appointed by the Lord), a Levite, ruler of the offerings and tithes in the time of Hezekiah. (<scripRef id="c-p207.1" passage="2 Chronicles 31:12" parsed="|2Chr|31|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.31.12">2 Chronicles 31:12</scripRef>,<scripRef passage="2 Chronicles 31:13" id="c-p207.2" parsed="|2Chr|31|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.31.13">13</scripRef>) (B.C. 726.)

This term (with one exception)— (<scripRef id="c-p209.1" passage="Isaiah 1:13" parsed="|Isa|1|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.1.13">Isaiah 1:13</scripRef>) is applied invariably to meetings of a religious character, in contradistinction to congregation.

As meet did not form an article of ordinary diet among the Jews, the art of cooking was not carried to any perfection. Few animals were slaughtered except for purposes of hospitality or festivity. The proceedings on such occasions appear to have been as follows:—On the arrival of a guest, the animal, either a kid, lamb or calf, was killed, (<scripRef id="c-p210.1" passage="Genesis 18:7" parsed="|Gen|18|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.18.7">Genesis 18:7</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p210.2" passage="Luke 15:23" parsed="|Luke|15|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.15.23">Luke 15:23</scripRef>) its throat being cut so that the blood might be poured out, (<scripRef id="c-p210.3" passage="Leviticus 7:26" parsed="|Lev|7|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.7.26">Leviticus 7:26</scripRef>) it was then flayed, and was ready for either roasting or boiling. In the former case the animal was preserved entire, (<scripRef id="c-p210.4" passage="Exodus 12:46" parsed="|Exod|12|46|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.12.46">Exodus 12:46</scripRef>) and roasted either over a fire, (<scripRef id="c-p210.5" passage="Exodus 12:8" parsed="|Exod|12|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.12.8">Exodus 12:8</scripRef>) of wood, (<scripRef id="c-p210.6" passage="Isaiah 44:16" parsed="|Isa|44|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.44.16">Isaiah 44:16</scripRef>) or perhaps in an oven, consisting simply of a hole dug in the earth, well heated, and covered up. Boiling, however, was the more usual method of cooking.
(Acts 21:1) [Cos, Or Coos]

Heb. nechosheth, in the Authorized Version always rendered “brass,” except in (<scripRef id="c-p212.1" passage="Ezra 8:27" parsed="|Ezra|8|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.8.27">Ezra 8:27</scripRef>) and <scripRef id="c-p212.2" passage="Jere 15:12" parsed="|Jer|15|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.15.12">Jere 15:12</scripRef> It was almost exclusively used by the ancients for common purposes, and for every kind of instrument, as chains, pillars, lavers and the other temple vessels. We read also of copper mirrors, (<scripRef id="c-p212.3" passage="Exodus 38:8" parsed="|Exod|38|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.38.8">Exodus 38:8</scripRef>) and even of copper arms, as helmets, spears, etc. (<scripRef id="c-p212.4" passage="1 Samuel 17:5" parsed="|1Sam|17|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.17.5">1 Samuel 17:5</scripRef>,<scripRef passage="1 Samuel 17:6" id="c-p212.5" parsed="|1Sam|17|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.17.6">6</scripRef>,<scripRef passage="1 Samuel 17:38" id="c-p212.6" parsed="|1Sam|17|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.17.38">38</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p212.7" passage="2 Samuel 21:16" parsed="|2Sam|21|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.21.16">2 Samuel 21:16</scripRef>)

(<scripRef id="c-p213.1" passage="Ezekiel 27:16" parsed="|Ezek|27|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.27.16">Ezekiel 27:16</scripRef>) A production of the sea, formed by minute animals called zoophytes. It is their shell or house. It takes various forms, as of trees, shrubs, hemispheres. The principal colors are red and white. It was used for beads and ornaments. With regard to the estimation in which coral was held by the Jews and other Orientals, it must be remembered that coral varies in price with us. Pliny says that the Indians valued coral as the Romans valued pearls. (<scripRef id="c-p213.2" passage="Job 28:18" parsed="|Job|28|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.28.18">Job 28:18</scripRef>)

an offering to God of any sort, bloody or bloodless, but particularly in fulfillment of a vow. The law laid down rules for vows, (1) affirmative; (2) negative. an ancient and celebrated city of Greece, on the Isthmus of Corinth, and about 40 miles west of Athens. In consequence of its geographical position it formed the most direct communication between the Ionian and AEgean seas. A remarkable feature was the AcroCorinthus, a vast citadel of rock, which rises abruptly to the height of 2000 feet above the level of the sea, and the summit of which is so extensive that it once contained a whole town. The situation of Corinth, and the possession of its eastern and western harbors, Cenchreae and Lechaeum, are the secrets of its history. Corinth was a place of great mental activity, as well as of commercial and manufacturing enterprise. Its wealth was so celebrated as to be proverbial; so were the vice and profligacy of its inhabitants. The worship of Venus where was attended with shameful licentiousness. Corinth is still an episcopal see. The city has now shrunk to a wretched village, ont he old site and bearing the old name, which, however, is corrupted into Gortho . St. Paul preached here, (Acts 18:11) and founded a church, to which his Epistles to the Corinthians are addressed. [EPISTLES TO THE Corinthians, First Epistle To The, Corinthians, Second Epistle To The]

was written by the apostle St. Paul toward the close of his nearly three-years stay at Ephesus, (<scripRef id="c-p219.1" passage="Acts 19:10" parsed="|Acts|19|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.19.10">Acts 19:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 20:31" id="c-p219.2" parsed="|Acts|20|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.20.31">20:31</scripRef>) which, we learn from (<scripRef id="c-p219.3" passage="1 Corinthians 16:8" parsed="|1Cor|16|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.16.8">1 Corinthians 16:8</scripRef>) probably terminated with the Pentecost of A.D. 57 or 58. The bearers were probably (according to the common subscription) Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus. It appears to have been called forth by the information the apostles had received of dissension in the Corinthian church, which may be thus explained:—The Corinthian church was planted by the apostle himself, (<scripRef id="c-p219.4" passage="1 Corinthians 3:6" parsed="|1Cor|3|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.3.6">1 Corinthians 3:6</scripRef>) in his second missionary journey. (<scripRef id="c-p219.5" passage="Acts 18:1" parsed="|Acts|18|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.18.1">Acts 18:1</scripRef>) seq. He abode in the city a year and a half. (<scripRef id="c-p219.6" passage="Acts 18:11" parsed="|Acts|18|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.18.11">Acts 18:11</scripRef>) A short time after the apostle had left the city the eloquent Jew of Alexandria, Apollos, went to Corinth, (<scripRef id="c-p219.7" passage="Acts 19:1" parsed="|Acts|19|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.19.1">Acts 19:1</scripRef>) and gained many followers, dividing the church into two parties, the followers of Paul and the followers of Apollos. Later on Judaizing teachers from Jerusalem preached the gospel in a spirit of direct antagonism to St. Paul personally. To this third party we may perhaps add a fourth, that, under the name of “the followers of Christ,” (<scripRef id="c-p219.8" passage="1 Corinthians 2:12" parsed="|1Cor|2|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.2.12">1 Corinthians 2:12</scripRef>) sought at first to separate themselves from the factious adherence to particular teachers, but eventually were driven by antagonism into positions equally sectarian and inimical to the unity of the church. At this momentous period, before parties had become consolidated and that distinctly withdrawn from communion with one another, the apostle writes; and in the outset of the epistle, <scripRef id="c-p219.9" passage="1Cor 1" parsed="|1Cor|1|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.1">1Cor 1</scripRef>-4:21, we have this noble and impassioned protest against this fourfold rending of the robe of Christ.

was written a few months subsequent to the first, in the same year—about the autumn of A.D. 57 or 58—at Macedonia. The epistle was occasioned by the information which the apostle had received form Titus, and also, as it would certainly seem probable, from Timothy, of the reception of the first epistle. This information, as it would seem from our present epistle, was mainly favorable; the better part of the church were returning to their spiritual allegiance to the founder, (<scripRef id="c-p220.1" passage="2 Corinthians 1:13" parsed="|2Cor|1|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.1.13">2 Corinthians 1:13</scripRef>,<scripRef passage="2 Corinthians 1:14" id="c-p220.2" parsed="|2Cor|1|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.1.14">14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Corinthians 7:9" id="c-p220.3" parsed="|2Cor|7|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.7.9">7:9</scripRef>,<scripRef passage="2 Corinthians 7:15" id="c-p220.4" parsed="|2Cor|7|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.7.15">15</scripRef>,<scripRef passage="2 Corinthians 7:16" id="c-p220.5" parsed="|2Cor|7|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.7.16">16</scripRef>) but there was still a faction who strenuously denied Paul’s claim to apostleship. The contents of this epistle comprise, (1) the apostle’s account of the character of his spiritual labors, chs. 1-7; (2) directions about the collections, chs. 8,9; (3) defence of his own apostolical character, chs. 10-13:10. The words in (<scripRef id="c-p220.6" passage="1 Corinthians 5:9" parsed="|1Cor|5|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.5.9">1 Corinthians 5:9</scripRef>) seem to point to further epistles to the church by Paul, but we have no positive evidence of any.

The “corner” of the field was not allowed, (<scripRef id="c-p224.1" passage="Leviticus 19:9" parsed="|Lev|19|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.19.9">Leviticus 19:9</scripRef>) to be wholly reaped. It formed a right of the poor to carry off what was so left, and this was a part of the maintenance from the soil to which that class were entitled. Under the scribes, minute legislation fixed one-sixtieth as the portion of a field which was to be left for the legal “corner.” The proportion being thus fixed, all the grain might be reaped, and enough to satisfy the regulation subsequently separated from the whole crop. This “corner” was, like the gleaning, tithe-free.

The Heb. berith means primarily “a cutting,” with reference to the custom of cutting or dividing animals in two and passing between the parts in ratifying a covenant. (Genesis 15; Jeremiah 34:18,19) In the New Testament the corresponding word is diathece (diatheke), which is frequently translated testament in the Authorized Version. In its biblical meaning two parties the word is used—

• Of a covenant between God and man; e.g. God covenanted with Noah, after the flood, that a like judgment should not be repeated. It is not precisely like a covenant between men, but was a promise or agreement by God. The principal covenants are the covenant of works—God promising to save and bless men on condition of perfect obedience—and the covenant of grace, or God’s promise to save men on condition of their believing in Christ and receiving him as their Master and Saviour. The first is called the Old Covenant, from which we name the first part of the bible the Old Testament, the Latin rendering of the word covenant. The second is called the New Covenant, or New Testament.

• Covenant between man and man, i.e. a solemn compact or agreement, either between tribes or nations, (Joshua 9:6,15; 1 Samuel 11:1) or between individuals, (Genesis 31:44) by which each party bound himself to fulfill certain conditions and was assured of receiving certain advantages. In making such a covenant God was solemnly invoked as witness, (Genesis 31:50) and an oath was sworn. (Genesis 21:31) A sign or witness of the covenant was sometimes framed, such a gift, (Genesis 21:30) or a pillar or heap of stones erected. (Genesis 31:52)

To create is to cause something to exist which did not exist before, as distinguished from make, to re-form something already in existence.

(The creation of all things is ascribed in the Bible to God, and is the only reasonable account of the origin of the world. The method of creation is not stated in Genesis, and as far as the account there is concerned, each part of it may be, after the first acts of creation, by evolution, or by direct act of God’s will. The word create (bara) is used but three times in the first chapter of Genesis— (1) as to the origin of matter; (2) as to the origin of life; (3) as to the origin of man’s soul; and science has always failed to do any of these acts thus ascribed to God. All other things are said to be made . The order of creation as given in Genesis is in close harmony with the order as revealed by geology, and the account there given, so long before the records of the rocks were read or the truth discoverable by man, is one of the strongest proofs that the Bible was inspired by God.—Ed.)

As the emblem of a slave’s death and a murderer’s punishment, the cross was naturally looked upon with the profoundest horror. But after the celebrated vision of Constantine, he ordered his friends to make a cross of gold and gems, such as he had seen, and “the towering eagles resigned the flags unto the cross,” and “the tree of cursing and shame” “sat upon the sceptres and was engraved and signed on the foreheads of kings.” (Jer. Taylor, “Life of Christ,” iii., xv. 1.) The new standards were called by the name Labarum, and may be seen on the coins of Constantine the Great and his nearer successors. The Latin cross on which our Lord suffered, was int he form of the letter T, and had an upright above the cross-bar, on which the “title” was placed. There was a projection from the central stem, on which the body of the sufferer rested. This was to prevent the weight of the body from tearing away the hands. Whether there was also a support to the feet (as we see in pictures) is doubtful. An inscription was generally placed above the criminal’s head, briefly expressing his guilt, and generally was carried before him. It was covered with white gypsum, and the letter were black.

This ornament, which is both ancient and universal, probably originated from the fillets used to prevent the hair from being dishevelled by the wind. Such fillets are still common; they gradually developed into turbans, which by the addition of ornamental or precious materials assumed the dignity of mitres or crowns. Both the ordinary priests and the high priest wore them. The crown was a symbol of royalty, and was worn by kings, (<scripRef id="c-p247.1" passage="2 Chronicles 23:11" parsed="|2Chr|23|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.23.11">2 Chronicles 23:11</scripRef>) and also by queens. (<scripRef id="c-p247.2" passage="Esther 2:17" parsed="|Esth|2|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Esth.2.17">Esther 2:17</scripRef>) The head-dress of bridegrooms, (<scripRef id="c-p247.3" passage="Ezekiel 24:17" parsed="|Ezek|24|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.24.17">Ezekiel 24:17</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p247.4" passage="Isaiah 61:10" parsed="|Isa|61|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.61.10">Isaiah 61:10</scripRef>) <scripRef id="c-p247.5" passage="Bar. 5:2" parsed="|Bar|5|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Bar.5.2">Bar. 5:2</scripRef>, and of women, (<scripRef id="c-p247.6" passage="Isaiah 3:20" parsed="|Isa|3|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.3.20">Isaiah 3:20</scripRef>) a head-dress of great splendor, (<scripRef id="c-p247.7" passage="Isaiah 28:5" parsed="|Isa|28|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.28.5">Isaiah 28:5</scripRef>) a wreath of flowers, (<scripRef id="c-p247.8" passage="Proverbs 1:9" parsed="|Prov|1|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.1.9">Proverbs 1:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Proverbs 4:9" id="c-p247.9" parsed="|Prov|4|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.4.9">4:9</scripRef>) denote crowns. In general we must attach to it the notion of a costly turban irradiated with pearls and gems of priceless value, which often form aigrettes for feathers, as in the crowns of modern Asiatics sovereigns. Such was probably the crown which weighed (or rather “was worth”) a talent, mentioned in (<scripRef id="c-p247.10" passage="2 Samuel 12:30" parsed="|2Sam|12|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.12.30">2 Samuel 12:30</scripRef>) taken by David from the king of Ammon at Rabbah, and used as the state crown of Judah. (<scripRef id="c-p247.11" passage="2 Samuel 12:30" parsed="|2Sam|12|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.12.30">2 Samuel 12:30</scripRef>) In (<scripRef id="c-p247.12" passage="Revelation 12:3" parsed="|Rev|12|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.12.3">Revelation 12:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Revelation 19:12" id="c-p247.13" parsed="|Rev|19|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.19.12">19:12</scripRef>) allusion is made to “many crowns” worn in token of extended dominion. The laurel, pine or parsley crowns given to victors int he great games of Greece are finely alluded to by St. Paul. (<scripRef id="c-p247.14" passage="1 Corinthians 9:25" parsed="|1Cor|9|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.9.25">1 Corinthians 9:25</scripRef>; <scripRef id="c-p247.15" passage="2 Timothy 2:5" parsed="|2Tim|2|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Tim.2.5">2 Timothy 2:5</scripRef>) etc.

(<scripRef id="c-p248.1" passage="Matthew 27:29" parsed="|Matt|27|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.27.29">Matthew 27:29</scripRef>) Our Lord was crowned with thorns in mockery by the Roman soldiers. Obviously some small flexile thorny shrub is meant perhaps Capparis spinosa. “Hasselquist, a Swedish naturalist, supposes a very common plant naba or nubka of the Arabs, with many small and sharp sines; soft, round and pliant branches; leaves much resembling ivy, of a very deep green, as if in designed mockery of a victor’s wreath.”—Alford.

was in used among the Egyptians, (<scripRef id="c-p249.1" passage="Genesis 40:19" parsed="|Gen|40|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.40.19">Genesis 40:19</scripRef>) the Carthaginians, the Persians, (<scripRef id="c-p249.2" passage="Esther 7:10" parsed="|Esth|7|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Esth.7.10">Esther 7:10</scripRef>) the Assyrians, Scythains, Indians, Germans, and from the earliest times among the Greeks and Romans. Whether this mode of execution was known to the ancient Jews is a matter of dispute. Probably the Jews borrowed it from the Romans. It was unanimously considered the most horrible form of death. Among the Romans the degradation was also a part of the infliction, and the punishment if applied to freemen was only used in the case of the vilest criminals. The one to be crucified was stripped naked of all his clothes, and then followed the most awful moment of all. He was laid down upon the implement of torture. His arms were stretched along the cross-beams, and at the centre of the open palms the point of a huge iron nail was placed, which, by the blow of a mallet, was driven home into the wood. Then through either foot separately, or possibly through both together, as they were placed one over the other, another huge nail tore its way through the quivering flesh. Whether the sufferer was also bound to the cross we do not know; but, to prevent the hands and feet being torn away by the weight of the body, which could not “rest upon nothing but four great wounds,” there was, about the centre of the cross, a wooden projection strong enough to support, at least in part, a human body, which soon became a weight of agony. Then the “accursed tree” with its living human burden was slowly heaved up and the end fixed firmly in a hole in the ground. The feet were but a little raised above the earth. The victim was in full reach of every hand that might choose to strike. A death by crucifixion seems to include all that pain and death can have of the horrible and ghastly,—dizziness, cramp, thirst, starvation, sleeplessness, traumatic fever, tetanus, publicity of shame, long continuance of torment, horror of anticipation, mortification of untended wounds, all intensified just up to the point at which they can be endured at all, but all stopping just short of the point which would give to the sufferer the relief of unconsciousness. The unnatural position made every movement painful; the lacerated veins and crushed tendons throbbed with incessant anguish; the wounds, inflamed by exposure, gradually gangrened; the arteries, especially of the head and stomach, became swollen and oppressed with surcharged blood; and, while each variety of misery went on gradually increasing, there was added to them the intolerable pang of a burning and raging thirst. Such was the death to which Christ was doomed.—Farrar’s “Life of Christ. ” The crucified was watched, according to custom, by a party of four soldiers, (<scripRef id="c-p249.3" passage="John 19:23" parsed="|John|19|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.19.23">John 19:23</scripRef>) with their centurion, (<scripRef id="c-p249.4" passage="Matthew 27:66" parsed="|Matt|27|66|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.27.66">Matthew 27:66</scripRef>) whose express office was to prevent the stealing of the body. This was necessary from the lingering character of the death, which sometimes did not supervene even for three days, and was at last the result of gradual benumbing and starvation. But for this guard, the persons might have been taken down and recovered, as was actually done in the case of a friend of Josephus. Fracture of the legs was especially adopted by the Jews to hasten death. (<scripRef id="c-p249.5" passage="John 19:31" parsed="|John|19|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.19.31">John 19:31</scripRef>) In most cases the body was suffered to rot on the cross by the action of sun and rain, or to be devoured by birds and beasts. Sepulture was generally therefore forbidden; but in consequence of (21:22,23) an express national exception was made in favor of the Jews. (<scripRef id="c-p249.6" passage="Matthew 27:58" parsed="|Matt|27|58|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.27.58">Matthew 27:58</scripRef>) This accursed and awful mode of punishment was happily abolished by Constantine.

a small vessel for holding water, such as was carried by Saul when on his night expedition after David, (<scripRef id="c-p250.1" passage="1 Samuel 26:11" parsed="|1Sam|26|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.26.11">1 Samuel 26:11</scripRef>,<scripRef passage="1 Samuel 26:12" id="c-p250.2" parsed="|1Sam|26|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.26.12">12</scripRef>,<scripRef passage="1 Samuel 26:16" id="c-p250.3" parsed="|1Sam|26|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.26.16">16</scripRef>) and by Elijah. the representative in the Authorized Version of two Hebrew words.
• Zecucith occurs only in (Job 28:17) where “glass” probably is intended.

• kerach occurs in numerous passages in the Old Testament to denote “ice,” “frost,” etc.; but once only (Ezekiel 1:22) as is generally understood, to signify “crystal.” The ancients supposed rock-crystal to be merely ice congealed by intense cold. The similarity of appearance between ice and crystal caused no doubt the identity of the terms to express these substances. The Greek word occurs in (Revelation 4:6; 21:1) It may mean either “ice” or “crystal.”
